title: Kindness beyond

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was nedivut, and your line was open hand. What did you give, and did it leave your hand gladly? Today, kindness that steps past the line. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-six.

A broken barrel of wine, and a court case. The Talmud, in tractate Bava Metzia, tells it. Some porters are carrying wine for a man named Rabbah bar bar Hanan, and they break a barrel. So he takes their cloaks to cover the loss. They go to Rav, the judge, and Rav tells him: give them back their cloaks. Rabbah asks the obvious question. Is that the law? The porters did break his barrel. Rav's answer, and what he says next, hold today's word.
screen: `A BROKEN BARREL.` → `GIVE BACK THE CLOAKS.` → `NOW PAY THEM TOO.`

segments.voice: Chesed. Loving-kindness, and in this block, the trait of kindness beyond what's owed. Turn it four ways. First, Rav's answer. Yes, he says, and he quotes Proverbs, in the old Jewish translation: "That thou mayest walk in the way of good men." The cloaks go back. Then the porters speak again: we're poor, we worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. Pay them their wages, says Rav. Is that the law? Yes, and he finishes the verse: "and keep the paths of the righteous." Rav holds Rabbah to a line past the strict one. Jewish tradition has a phrase for that: lifnim mishurat hadin, inside the line of the law: not breaking the law, but stepping back from what you're entitled to. Second, chesed is larger than charity. The Talmud, in tractate Sukkah, says acts of loving-kindness are greater than charity in three ways. Charity is given with money; kindness with your body too. Charity goes to the poor; kindness to poor and rich alike. Charity is for the living; kindness reaches the living and the dead. Third, the world leans on it. Pirkei Avot keeps a saying of Simon the Just: the world stands on three things, on Torah, on worship, and on acts of loving-kindness. Fourth, it doesn't keep a bill. Owed kindness keeps accounts: I helped you, so you help me. Chesed goes past the account. The same verse of Micah that asked us to walk humbly, back on humility day, also asks "to love mercy," and the Hebrew word behind mercy there is chesed. Not to tolerate it. To love it. Yesterday's generosity opened the hand. Chesed keeps it open after the bill is paid.
screen: `INSIDE THE LINE OF THE LAW.` · `GREATER THAN CHARITY IN THREE WAYS.` · `THE WORLD STANDS ON KINDNESS.` · `NO BILL, NO ACCOUNT.` · then, large: `TO LOVE MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one extra kindness. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place in your life where you're owed something, or where you only owe the minimum. A neighbor, a coworker, a delivery driver, someone who made a mistake that cost you. Now look one step past the line. What would it look like to give a little more than the rule asks? Wave off a small debt. Stay five more minutes. Say thank you to someone who was only doing their job. Choose one, and see the moment clearly. If you pray, you can carry that person into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Chesed. Loving-kindness: giving past what's owed, with your body and your time as well as your money, to anyone at all. Today's word.
Your line: beyond what's owed. Today, do the one extra kindness you chose, and don't mention it afterward. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Jewish communities organize acts of loving-kindness, gemilut chasadim, such as free loan societies, meals for mourners and new parents, and visits to the sick, and Mussar students practice chesed by going one step past what's required.

fork.setup: you're Rav. porters broke a barrel of wine, and the owner kept their cloaks. they say they're poor and hungry. what do you rule?
options: they owe for the wine; he keeps the cloaks.
return the cloaks, and pay them their wages.
split the loss down the middle.
fork.reveal: Rav rules both, quoting Proverbs a half-verse at a time: "That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous."

trapdoor: what you thought: chesed means being nice.
what it means: kindness past what's owed, with body and time as well as money, to anyone, living or dead.
what a scholar hears: Bava Metzia 83a and lifnim mishurat hadin; Sukkah 49b on kindness and charity; Micah's ahavat chesed, rendered to love mercy.

notes: Editor pass: Bava Metzia 83a sequence corrected (Rabbah asks 'is that the law?' after each ruling, and Rav answers with each half of Proverbs 2:20 in turn); 'the rabbis' phrase' changed to 'Jewish tradition has a phrase' since 83a does not use lifnim mishurat hadin; the Micah line now calls back to day 1256 instead of repeating it as new.
Bava Metzia 83a (Rabbah bar bar Hanan and the porters, Rav quoting Proverbs 2:20): paraphrased; confirm details (cloaks, wages, 'is that the law?').
The term lifnim mishurat hadin is linked here to the story; the Talmud's discussion of it is at Bava Metzia 30b. Confirm the link is fair.
Proverbs 2:20 and Micah 6:8 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.
Sukkah 49b: the three ways loving-kindness is greater than charity, paraphrased; confirm.
